messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: SEM problem
parts: 1- Is it necessary that I run bivariate regression between all variables?
No, the advantage of SEM is that you can fit all regression models simultaneously.
2-some of my variables are in the different ranges and scales, such as longitude, latitude, slope, elevation, .... I transformed these measured variable  to the log format

Why?  That doesn't change the fact that different variables are measured on different scales, nor is it a necessarily a problem that different variables are on different scale.  To avoid the warning you see about different variances, you can rescale variables by multiplying/dividing by a constant (e.g., to express elevation in kilometers instead of meters).

It is a BIG problem when you can't interpret your estimates because you are trying to model nonlinear effects on log-transformed variables (e.g., exponentiated slopes would need to be interpreted as multiplicative effects, SEs are not necessarily correct).  If you want to include complicated link functions or nonlinear effects, Bayesian SEM would provide a much more flexible modeling framework.

#laten variable

topography =~ X + Y + E + S

X, Y, E and S are longitude, latitude, elevation and slope, Respectively.


Does this make any sense?  Longitude, latitude, and elevation are not caused by topography (or location), they ARE location along different axes/dimensions.  It wouldn't make any sense to say "When topography increases by 1 unit, longitude, latitude, elevation, and slope all increase by [their factor loadings] units".  Perhaps a composite (formative construct) is what you had in mind?
